Reference: Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021)

Model Setting

The paper develops identification, aggregation, estimation and inference for Difference-in-Differences (DiD) designs with (i) more than two time periods, (ii) variation in treatment timing (staggered adoption), and (iii) a parallel trends assumption that may hold only after conditioning on pre-treatment covariates. The analysis is deliberately split into three steps. The identification step targets a disaggregated causal parameter, the group-time average treatment effect ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t), the average effect at time ttt for the units first treated in period ggg. The aggregation step combines the ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t) with explicit non-negative weights into event-study, group-specific, calendar-time and overall summary parameters. The estimation step uses two-step plug-in estimators with parametric first steps and a multiplier bootstrap that delivers simultaneous confidence bands. Because the building blocks do not restrict heterogeneity across groups, across time or in covariates, the approach avoids the problems of interpreting two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regressions under heterogeneous and dynamic treatment effects documented by Borusyak and Jaravel (2017), de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020), Goodman-Bacon (2019) and Sun and Abraham (2020).

The main results are as follows. Under limited anticipation, a conditional parallel trends assumption and overlap, every ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t) is nonparametrically point-identified, and it can be written equivalently as an outcome regression (OR), an inverse probability weighting (IPW) or a doubly robust (DR) estimand, using either the never-treated units or the not-yet-treated units as the comparison group (Theorem 1). The DR plug-in estimators are n\sqrt{n}n​-consistent and jointly asymptotically normal when either the propensity score model or the outcome regression model is correctly specified (Theorem 2), and the multiplier bootstrap is valid (Theorem 3). In an application to state minimum wage increases and county teen employment in 2001-2007, the proposed estimator under conditional parallel trends gives an overall effect of −0.031-0.031−0.031, whereas the corresponding TWFE coefficient is −0.008-0.008−0.008 and insignificant.

Group-Time Average Treatment Effect

In the canonical setup with two periods and two groups the parameter of interest is ATT=E[Y2(2)−Y2(0)∣G2=1]ATT=\mathbb{E}[Y_2(2)-Y_2(0)|G_2=1]ATT=E[Y2​(2)−Y2​(0)∣G2​=1]. Its generalization is:

ATT(g,t)=E[Yt(g)−Yt(0)∣Gg=1](3)ATT(g,t)=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_t(g)-Y_t(0)|G_g=1\right] \tag{3}ATT(g,t)=E[Yt​(g)−Yt​(0)∣Gg​=1](3)

The family of ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t) imposes no restriction on how effects vary across groups or over time. Fixing ggg and varying ttt traces the dynamics of the effect for one group, and comparing groups shows how those dynamics differ by adoption date. The first line is Assumption 4 (never-treated comparison group) and holds for each g∈Gg\in\mathcal{G}g∈G and t∈{2,…,T}t\in\{2,\dots,\mathcal{T}\}t∈{2,…,T} with t≥g−δt\geq g-\deltat≥g−δ. The second line is Assumption 5 (not-yet-treated comparison groups) and holds for each g∈Gg\in\mathcal{G}g∈G and each pair (s,t)(s,t)(s,t) with t≥g−δt\geq g-\deltat≥g−δ and t+δ≤s<gˉt+\delta\leq s<\bar{g}t+δ≤s<gˉ​. Both allow covariate-specific trends, which matters when the distribution of XXX differs across groups and the path of untreated outcomes depends on XXX, and neither restricts the relation between treatment timing and Yt(g)Y_t(g)Yt​(g), so both are weaker than random adoption dates. Their unconditional versions are weaker than the parallel trends assumptions of de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020) and Sun and Abraham (2020) because they place fewer restrictions on pre-treatment periods.

The choice between the two involves a trade-off. Assumption 4 is attractive when a sizeable never-treated group exists and resembles the eventually treated units. Assumption 5 uses more comparison units and is the only option when there is no (or a very small) never-treated group, but with δ=0\delta=0δ=0 it restricts pre-treatment trends across groups, which Assumption 4 does not. The authors advise against choosing between them with statistical pre-tests, citing Roth (2020). A further trade-off links anticipation and parallel trends: as δ\deltaδ rises, parallel trends must hold in more pre-treatment periods, so the assumptions become stronger. Finally, Assumption 6 (overlap) requires that for each t∈{2,…,T}t\in\{2,\dots,\mathcal{T}\}t∈{2,…,T} and g∈Gg\in\mathcal{G}g∈G there is some ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 with P(Gg=1)>εP(G_g=1)>\varepsilonP(Gg​=1)>ε and pg,t(X)<1−εp_{g,t}(X)<1-\varepsilonpg,t​(X)<1−ε almost surely: a positive fraction of the population starts treatment in each period ggg and the generalized propensity score is bounded away from one.

The theorem extends the OR approach of Heckman, Ichimura and Todd (1997), the IPW approach of Abadie (2005) and the DR approach of Sant'Anna and Zhao (2020) to many groups and periods. It resolves two questions. The reference period is g−δ−1g-\delta-1g−δ−1, the most recent period in which untreated potential outcomes of group ggg are observed; more anticipation pushes it further back. The comparison group follows from the parallel trends assumption: the never-treated units serve as a fixed comparison group for every ggg under Assumption 4, and the units not yet treated by t+δt+\deltat+δ serve as a comparison group that changes with ttt under Assumption 5. When all units are eventually treated (gˉ<∞\bar{g}<\inftygˉ​<∞), effects are identified only for t<gˉ−δt<\bar{g}-\deltat<gˉ​−δ and not for the last cohort. Anticipation costs the early groups outside Gδ\mathcal{G}_\deltaGδ​ and the last δ\deltaδ periods, although the latter can be recovered when some units are known to remain untreated beyond T\mathcal{T}T. The three estimands coincide in the population but rely on different parts of the data generating process, which matters for estimation. Covariates must be pre-treatment variables associated with the evolution of Y(0)Y(0)Y(0); post-treatment covariates are excluded.

Why TWFE Fails and the Aggregation Framework

Applied work usually summarizes effects with the static and dynamic TWFE specifications:

Yi,t=αt+αg+βDi,t+ϵi,tYi,t=αt+αg+∑e=−K−2δeanticip⋅Di,te+∑e=0Lβe⋅Di,te+vi,t(13)\begin{aligned} Y_{i,t}&=\alpha_t+\alpha_g+\beta D_{i,t}+\epsilon_{i,t}\\ Y_{i,t}&=\alpha_t+\alpha_g+\sum_{e=-K}^{-2}\delta^{anticip}_e\cdot D^e_{i,t}+\sum_{e=0}^{L}\beta_e\cdot D^e_{i,t}+v_{i,t} \end{aligned} \tag{13}Yi,t​Yi,t​​=αt​+αg​+βDi,t​+ϵi,t​=αt​+αg​+e=−K∑−2​δeanticip​⋅Di,te​+e=0∑L​βe​⋅Di,te​+vi,t​​(13)

where αt\alpha_tαt​ and αg\alpha_gαg​ are time and group fixed effects, Di,te=1{t−Gi=e}D^e_{i,t}=\mathbf{1}\{t-G_i=e\}Di,te​=1{t−Gi​=e} indicates that unit iii is eee periods away from first treatment, and KKK and LLL are positive constants. In general β\betaβ is a weighted average of underlying effects in which some weights can be negative, so β\betaβ can be negative even when the effect is positive for every unit; the problem arises when effects evolve over time, because already-treated units act as controls. Even non-negative weights are dictated by the estimation method and depend on group sizes, treatment timing and the number of periods. Sun and Abraham (2020) show that the βe\beta_eβe​ of the dynamic specification suffer from similar problems. The paper instead forms aggregates with weights chosen by the researcher:

θ=∑g∈G∑t=2Tw(g,t)⋅ATT(g,t)(14)\theta=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{t=2}^{\mathcal{T}}w(g,t)\cdot ATT(g,t) \tag{14}θ=g∈G∑​t=2∑T​w(g,t)⋅ATT(g,t)(14)

where w(g,t)w(g,t)w(g,t) are known or estimable weighting functions chosen so that θ\thetaθ answers a well-posed question. For the aggregation schemes the paper sets δ=0\delta=0δ=0 and assumes that a never-treated group exists.

Aggregation Schemes

Length of exposure. The event-study parameter is:

θes(e)=∑g∈G1{g+e≤T}P(G=g∣G+e≤T)ATT(g,g+e)(15)\theta_{es}(e)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{1}\{g+e\leq\mathcal{T}\}P(G=g|G+e\leq\mathcal{T})ATT(g,g+e) \tag{15}θes​(e)=g∈G∑​1{g+e≤T}P(G=g∣G+e≤T)ATT(g,g+e)(15)

the average effect eee periods after adoption across all groups that are observed for exactly eee periods of exposure, weighted by group size; e=0e=0e=0 is the effect on impact. It is the natural target of event-study regressions. Comparisons across eee can be contaminated by composition: for 0≤e1<e2≤T−20\leq e_1<e_2\leq\mathcal{T}-20≤e1​<e2​≤T−2 the difference θes(e2)−θes(e1)\theta_{es}(e_2)-\theta_{es}(e_1)θes​(e2​)−θes​(e1​) equals a weighted average of the true dynamic effects ATT(g,g+e2)−ATT(g,g+e1)ATT(g,g+e_2)-ATT(g,g+e_1)ATT(g,g+e2​)−ATT(g,g+e1​) plus two terms that reflect different group weights and different sets of groups at the two event times. These terms vanish only if ATT(g,g+e)ATT(g,g+e)ATT(g,g+e) does not vary with ggg. The balanced version fixes the set of groups: for 0≤e≤e′≤T−20\leq e\leq e'\leq\mathcal{T}-20≤e≤e′≤T−2,

θesbal(e;e′)=∑g∈G1{g+e′≤T}ATT(g,g+e)P(G=g∣G+e′≤T)(16)\theta^{bal}_{es}(e;e')=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{1}\{g+e'\leq\mathcal{T}\}ATT(g,g+e)P(G=g|G+e'\leq\mathcal{T}) \tag{16}θesbal​(e;e′)=g∈G∑​1{g+e′≤T}ATT(g,g+e)P(G=g∣G+e′≤T)(16)

which averages over groups exposed for at least e′e'e′ periods. Differences across eee are then free of composition effects, at the price of using fewer groups (a robustness versus efficiency trade-off).

Groups. Heterogeneity by adoption date is summarized by:

θsel(g~)=1T−g~+1∑t=g~TATT(g~,t)(17)\theta_{sel}(\tilde{g})=\frac{1}{\mathcal{T}-\tilde{g}+1}\sum_{t=\tilde{g}}^{\mathcal{T}}ATT(\tilde{g},t) \tag{17}θsel​(g~​)=T−g~​+11​t=g~​∑T​ATT(g~​,t)(17)

the average effect for group g~\tilde{g}g~​ across all its post-treatment periods.

Calendar time. The average effect in period ttt among groups treated by ttt, and its cumulative version, are:

θc(t)=∑g∈G1{t≥g}P(G=g∣G≤t)ATT(g,t),θccumu(t~)=∑t=2t~θc(t)(18)\theta_c(t)=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{1}\{t\geq g\}P(G=g|G\leq t)ATT(g,t),\qquad\theta^{cumu}_c(\tilde{t})=\sum_{t=2}^{\tilde{t}}\theta_c(t) \tag{18}θc​(t)=g∈G∑​1{t≥g}P(G=g∣G≤t)ATT(g,t),θccumu​(t~)=t=2∑t~​θc​(t)(18)

The cumulative parameter measures, for instance, total earnings gains from a training program up to year t~\tilde{t}t~. All partial aggregates have non-negative weights that sum to one, except θccumu(t~)\theta^{cumu}_c(\tilde{t})θccumu​(t~), whose weights sum to t~−1\tilde{t}-1t~−1.

Overall Summary Parameters

The simplest overall parameter averages all identified group-time effects:

θWO=1κ∑g∈G∑t=2T1{t≥g}ATT(g,t)P(G=g∣G≤T),κ=∑g∈G∑t=2T1{t≥g}P(G=g∣G≤T)(19)\theta^O_W=\frac{1}{\kappa}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{t=2}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathbf{1}\{t\geq g\}ATT(g,t)P(G=g|G\leq\mathcal{T}),\qquad\kappa=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{t=2}^{\mathcal{T}}\mathbf{1}\{t\geq g\}P(G=g|G\leq\mathcal{T}) \tag{19}θWO​=κ1​g∈G∑​t=2∑T​1{t≥g}ATT(g,t)P(G=g∣G≤T),κ=g∈G∑​t=2∑T​1{t≥g}P(G=g∣G≤T)(19)

Unlike β\betaβ it cannot be negative when all effects are positive, but it systematically puts more weight on groups that are treated for longer. The recommended general-purpose summary is:

θselO=∑g∈Gθsel(g)P(G=g∣G≤T)(20)\theta^O_{sel}=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\theta_{sel}(g)P(G=g|G\leq\mathcal{T}) \tag{20}θselO​=g∈G∑​θsel​(g)P(G=g∣G≤T)(20)

which first averages over time within each group and then across groups by group size. It is the average effect experienced by all units that ever participate in the treatment, the same interpretation as the ATTATTATT in the two-period, two-group case. Overall parameters can also be built from the event-study and calendar-time aggregates:

θesO=1T−1∑e=0T−2θes(e),θcO=1T−1∑t=2Tθc(t),θesO,bal(e′)=1e′+1∑e=0e′θesbal(e;e′)(21)\theta^O_{es}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{T}-1}\sum_{e=0}^{\mathcal{T}-2}\theta_{es}(e),\qquad\theta^O_c=\frac{1}{\mathcal{T}-1}\sum_{t=2}^{\mathcal{T}}\theta_c(t),\qquad\theta^{O,bal}_{es}(e')=\frac{1}{e'+1}\sum_{e=0}^{e'}\theta^{bal}_{es}(e;e') \tag{21}θesO​=T−11​e=0∑T−2​θes​(e),θcO​=T−11​t=2∑T​θc​(t),θesO,bal​(e′)=e′+11​e=0∑e′​θesbal​(e;e′)(21)

The first two inherit the composition problem; the third avoids it but is local to groups exposed for at least e′e'e′ periods. None of the overall parameters coincide in general. They are all equal, and equal to β\betaβ, in the special case where ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t) is the same for all groups and periods, and generally differ otherwise.

Estimation

Identification is constructive and suggests a two-step strategy. In the first step the nuisance functions are estimated for each (g,t)(g,t)(g,t): pg(⋅)p_g(\cdot)pg​(⋅) and mg,t,δnev(⋅)m^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}(\cdot)mg,t,δnev​(⋅) under Assumption 4, or pg,t+δ(⋅)p_{g,t+\delta}(\cdot)pg,t+δ​(⋅) and mg,t,δny(⋅)m^{ny}_{g,t,\delta}(\cdot)mg,t,δny​(⋅) under Assumption 5. In the second step fitted values are plugged into the sample analogue of the estimand. The OR approach requires a correct model for the outcome evolution of the comparison group, the IPW approach a correct model for the generalized propensity score, and the DR approach requires only one of the two to be correct. The paper therefore works with the DR estimator and parametric first steps (for example a logit and a linear regression), which are practical when the number of covariates is large relative to the sample; nonparametric first steps would need convergence faster than n−1/4n^{-1/4}n−1/4. With the never-treated comparison group:

ATT^drnev(g,t;δ)=En[(w^gtreat−w^gcomp,nev)(Yt−Yg−δ−1−m^g,t,δnev(X;β^g,t,δnev))](22)\widehat{ATT}^{nev}_{dr}(g,t;\delta)=\mathbb{E}_n\left[\left(\widehat{w}^{treat}_g-\widehat{w}^{comp,nev}_g\right)\left(Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}-\widehat{m}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\left(X;\widehat{\beta}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)\right)\right] \tag{22}ATTdrnev​(g,t;δ)=En​[(wgtreat​−wgcomp,nev​)(Yt​−Yg−δ−1​−mg,t,δnev​(X;β​g,t,δnev​))](22)

with weights:

w^gtreat=GgEn[Gg],w^gcomp,nev=p^g(X;π^g)C1−p^g(X;π^g)En[p^g(X;π^g)C1−p^g(X;π^g)](23)\widehat{w}^{treat}_g=\frac{G_g}{\mathbb{E}_n\left[G_g\right]},\qquad\widehat{w}^{comp,nev}_g=\frac{\dfrac{\widehat{p}_g\left(X;\widehat{\pi}_g\right)C}{1-\widehat{p}_g\left(X;\widehat{\pi}_g\right)}}{\mathbb{E}_n\left[\dfrac{\widehat{p}_g\left(X;\widehat{\pi}_g\right)C}{1-\widehat{p}_g\left(X;\widehat{\pi}_g\right)}\right]} \tag{23}wgtreat​=En​[Gg​]Gg​​,wgcomp,nev​=En​[1−p​g​(X;πg​)p​g​(X;πg​)C​]1−p​g​(X;πg​)p​g​(X;πg​)C​​(23)

where En[Z]=n−1∑i=1nZi\mathbb{E}_n[Z]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_iEn​[Z]=n−1∑i=1n​Zi​, and p^g(⋅;π^g)\widehat{p}_g(\cdot;\widehat{\pi}_g)p​g​(⋅;πg​) and m^g,t,δnev(⋅;β^g,t,δnev)\widehat{m}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}(\cdot;\widehat{\beta}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta})mg,t,δnev​(⋅;β​g,t,δnev​) are the parametric estimators of the propensity score and the outcome regression. The estimator ATT^drny(g,t;δ)\widehat{ATT}^{ny}_{dr}(g,t;\delta)ATTdrny​(g,t;δ) is defined in the same way with w^gcomp,ny\widehat{w}^{comp,ny}_gwgcomp,ny​, which uses p^g,t+δ(X;π^g,t+δ)\widehat{p}_{g,t+\delta}(X;\widehat{\pi}_{g,t+\delta})p​g,t+δ​(X;πg,t+δ​) and (1−Dt+δ)(1−Gg)(1-D_{t+\delta})(1-G_g)(1−Dt+δ​)(1−Gg​), and with m^g,t,δny(X;β^g,t,δny)\widehat{m}^{ny}_{g,t,\delta}(X;\widehat{\beta}^{ny}_{g,t,\delta})mg,t,δny​(X;β​g,t,δny​). The weights are of the Hajek type and sum to one in finite samples, which usually improves finite sample behaviour. Aggregated parameters are estimated by the analogy principle. With limited overlap (propensity scores close to one) IPW and DR estimators can be imprecise; the OR estimator, which extrapolates parametrically, may then be more informative, while trimming changes the target parameter.

Asymptotic Theory

The theory is stated for the never-treated case in a large nnn, fixed T\mathcal{T}T framework. Let W=(Y1,…,YT,X,D1,…,DT)W=(Y_1,\dots,Y_{\mathcal{T}},X,D_1,\dots,D_{\mathcal{T}})W=(Y1​,…,YT​,X,D1​,…,DT​) and let κg,tnev=(πg′,βg,t,δnev′)′\kappa^{nev}_{g,t}=(\pi_g',\beta^{nev\prime}_{g,t,\delta})'κg,tnev​=(πg′​,βg,t,δnev′​)′ collect the first-step parameters, with pseudo-true value κg,t∗,nev\kappa^{*,nev}_{g,t}κg,t∗,nev​. Assumption 7 requires smooth parametric working models with a unique pseudo-true parameter in the interior of a compact set and first-step estimators that are strongly consistent and asymptotically linear, with propensity scores bounded away from one; Assumption 8 imposes integrability conditions. Logit or probit models and linear or nonlinear regressions estimated by quasi-maximum likelihood or least squares satisfy them. The influence function of the DR estimator is:

with components:

ψg,t,δtreat,nev(W;βg,t,δnev)=wgtreat⋅(Yt−Yg−δ−1−mg,t,δnev(βg,t,δnev))−wgtreat⋅E[wgtreat⋅(Yt−Yg−δ−1−mg,t,δnev(βg,t,δnev))]ψg,t,δcomp,nev(W;πg,βg,t,δnev)=wgcomp(πg)⋅(Yt−Yg−δ−1−mg,t,δnev(βg,t,δnev))−wgcomp(πg)⋅E[wgcomp(πg)⋅(Yt−Yg−δ−1−mg,t,δnev(βg,t,δnev))]ψg,t,δest,nev(W;πg,βg,t,δnev)=lg,tor,nev(βg,t,δnev)′⋅Mg,t,δdr,nev,1+lgps,nev(πg)′⋅Mg,t,δdr,nev,2(25)\begin{aligned} \psi^{treat,nev}_{g,t,\delta}(W;\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta})&=w^{treat}_g\cdot\left(Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}-m^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\left(\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)\right)-w^{treat}_g\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[w^{treat}_g\cdot\left(Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}-m^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\left(\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)\right)\right]\\ \psi^{comp,nev}_{g,t,\delta}(W;\pi_g,\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta})&=w^{comp}_g\left(\pi_g\right)\cdot\left(Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}-m^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\left(\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)\right)-w^{comp}_g\left(\pi_g\right)\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[w^{comp}_g\left(\pi_g\right)\cdot\left(Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}-m^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\left(\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)\right)\right]\\ \psi^{est,nev}_{g,t,\delta}(W;\pi_g,\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta})&=l^{or,nev}_{g,t}\left(\beta^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)'\cdot M^{dr,nev,1}_{g,t,\delta}+l^{ps,nev}_g\left(\pi_g\right)'\cdot M^{dr,nev,2}_{g,t,\delta} \end{aligned} \tag{25}ψg,t,δtreat,nev​(W;βg,t,δnev​)ψg,t,δcomp,nev​(W;πg​,βg,t,δnev​)ψg,t,δest,nev​(W;πg​,βg,t,δnev​)​=wgtreat​⋅(Yt​−Yg−δ−1​−mg,t,δnev​(βg,t,δnev​))−wgtreat​⋅E[wgtreat​⋅(Yt​−Yg−δ−1​−mg,t,δnev​(βg,t,δnev​))]=wgcomp​(πg​)⋅(Yt​−Yg−δ−1​−mg,t,δnev​(βg,t,δnev​))−wgcomp​(πg​)⋅E[wgcomp​(πg​)⋅(Yt​−Yg−δ−1​−mg,t,δnev​(βg,t,δnev​))]=lg,tor,nev​(βg,t,δnev​)′⋅Mg,t,δdr,nev,1​+lgps,nev​(πg​)′⋅Mg,t,δdr,nev,2​​(25)

The linear representation follows from the two-period result of Sant'Anna and Zhao (2020) applied to each (g,t)(g,t)(g,t), and joint normality from the Lindeberg-Levy central limit theorem. Multiplier Bootstrap and Simultaneous Confidence Bands

A plug-in estimate of Σ\SigmaΣ would give pointwise intervals. The paper instead proposes a multiplier bootstrap. Let Ψ^t≥(g−δ)dr,nev(W)\widehat{\Psi}^{dr,nev}_{t\geq(g-\delta)}(W)Ψt≥(g−δ)dr,nev​(W) be the sample analogue of the stacked influence function and let {Vi}i=1n\{V_i\}_{i=1}^n{Vi​}i=1n​ be independent and identically distributed draws with zero mean, unit variance and finite third moment, independent of the data, for example the two-point distribution of Mammen (1993). A bootstrap draw and its limit (Theorem 3, under the assumptions of Theorem 2) are:

ATT^t≥(g−δ)∗,dr,nev=ATT^t≥(g−δ)dr,nev+En[V⋅Ψ^t≥(g−δ)dr,nev(W)]n(ATT^t≥(g−δ)∗,dr,nev−ATT^t≥(g−δ)dr,nev)→∗dN(0,Σ)(27)\begin{aligned} \widehat{ATT}^{*,dr,nev}_{t\geq(g-\delta)}&=\widehat{ATT}^{dr,nev}_{t\geq(g-\delta)}+\mathbb{E}_n\left[V\cdot\widehat{\Psi}^{dr,nev}_{t\geq(g-\delta)}(W)\right]\\ \sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{ATT}^{*,dr,nev}_{t\geq(g-\delta)}-\widehat{ATT}^{dr,nev}_{t\geq(g-\delta)}\right)&\xrightarrow[*]{d}N(0,\Sigma) \end{aligned} \tag{27}ATTt≥(g−δ)∗,dr,nev​n​(ATTt≥(g−δ)∗,dr,nev​−ATTt≥(g−δ)dr,nev​)​=ATTt≥(g−δ)dr,nev​+En​[V⋅Ψt≥(g−δ)dr,nev​(W)]d∗​N(0,Σ)​(27)

where the starred arrow denotes weak convergence of the bootstrap law in probability, conditional on the original sample; the same holds for any continuous functional of the left-hand side. The proof combines the conditional multiplier central limit theorem with a demonstration that replacing the true influence function by its estimate has a negligible effect. Each draw only perturbs the estimated influence function, so nothing is re-estimated, every draw contains observations from every group, and simultaneous confidence bands are easy to compute. Algorithm 1: (1) draw {Vi}i=1n\{V_i\}_{i=1}^n{Vi​}i=1n​; (2) compute the bootstrap draw and, for each (g,t)(g,t)(g,t), R^∗(g,t)\widehat{R}^*(g,t)R∗(g,t); (3) repeat BBB times; (4) estimate the standard errors from the bootstrap interquartile range; (5) for each draw compute the maximal studentized statistic and take c^1−α\widehat{c}_{1-\alpha}c1−α​ as the empirical (1−α)(1-\alpha)(1−α)-quantile of this maximum over the BBB draws; (6) form the band. In symbols:

R^∗(g,t)=n(ATT^∗(g,t)−ATT^(g,t)),Σ^1/2(g,t)=q0.75(g,t)−q0.25(g,t)z0.75−z0.25t-testt≥(g−δ)=max⁡(g,t)∣R^∗(g,t)∣Σ^(g,t)−1/2,C^(g,t)=[ATT^drnev(g,t;δ)±c^1−αΣ^(g,t)1/2/n](28)\begin{aligned} \widehat{R}^*(g,t)&=\sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{ATT}^*(g,t)-\widehat{ATT}(g,t)\right),\qquad\widehat{\Sigma}^{1/2}(g,t)=\frac{q_{0.75}(g,t)-q_{0.25}(g,t)}{z_{0.75}-z_{0.25}}\\ \text{t-test}_{t\geq(g-\delta)}&=\max_{(g,t)}\left|\widehat{R}^*(g,t)\right|\widehat{\Sigma}(g,t)^{-1/2},\qquad\widehat{C}(g,t)=\left[\widehat{ATT}^{nev}_{dr}(g,t;\delta)\pm\widehat{c}_{1-\alpha}\widehat{\Sigma}(g,t)^{1/2}/\sqrt{n}\right] \end{aligned} \tag{28}R∗(g,t)t-testt≥(g−δ)​​=n​(ATT∗(g,t)−ATT(g,t)),Σ1/2(g,t)=z0.75​−z0.25​q0.75​(g,t)−q0.25​(g,t)​=(g,t)max​​R∗(g,t)​Σ(g,t)−1/2,C(g,t)=[ATTdrnev​(g,t;δ)±c1−α​Σ(g,t)1/2/n​]​(28)

where qp(g,t)q_p(g,t)qp​(g,t) is the pppth sample quantile of R^∗(g,t)\widehat{R}^*(g,t)R∗(g,t) across the BBB draws and zpz_pzp​ is the pppth quantile of the standard normal distribution. (The paper prints the exponent of Σ^(g,t)\widehat{\Sigma}(g,t)Σ(g,t) in the band as −1/2-1/2−1/2; the band is written here with the standard error, as the construction requires.) Corollary 1 states that the band covers all ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t) with g∈Gδg\in\mathcal{G}_\deltag∈Gδ​ and t≥g−δt\geq g-\deltat≥g−δ jointly with probability converging to 1−α1-\alpha1−α. Unlike pointwise intervals, the band does not suffer from multiple-testing problems. Setting Σ^(g,t)=1\widehat{\Sigma}(g,t)=1Σ(g,t)=1 gives a valid band of constant width that may be longer. For cluster-robust inference one draws one multiplier per cluster instead of one per observation, which is justified when the number of clusters is large.

Inference for Aggregated Parameters

With δ=0\delta=0δ=0, the plug-in estimator of an aggregated parameter and the required expansion of the estimated weights are:

where ξg,tw\xi^w_{g,t}ξg,tw​ has mean zero and finite variance; sample analogues of all the weights above satisfy this condition. Corollary 2 states that, under the assumptions of Theorem 2:

lw(Wi)=∑g∈G∑t=2T(w(g,t)⋅ψg,t,0dr,nev(Wi;κg,t∗,nev)+ξg,tw(Wi)⋅ATT(g,t))n(θ^−θ)=1n∑i=1nlw(Wi)+op(1)→dN(0,E[lw(W)2])(30)\begin{aligned} l^w(W_i)&=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{t=2}^{\mathcal{T}}\left(w(g,t)\cdot\psi^{dr,nev}_{g,t,0}(W_i;\kappa^{*,nev}_{g,t})+\xi^w_{g,t}(W_i)\cdot ATT(g,t)\right)\\ \sqrt{n}\left(\widehat{\theta}-\theta\right)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^nl^w(W_i)+o_p(1)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\mathbb{E}\left[l^w(W)^2\right]\right) \end{aligned} \tag{30}lw(Wi​)n​(θ−θ)​=g∈G∑​t=2∑T​(w(g,t)⋅ψg,t,0dr,nev​(Wi​;κg,t∗,nev​)+ξg,tw​(Wi​)⋅ATT(g,t))=n​1​i=1∑n​lw(Wi​)+op​(1)d​N(0,E[lw(W)2])​(30)

The influence function of an aggregate has two parts: the weighted influence functions of the group-time estimators, and the contribution of estimating the weights (group shares). Inference can use a consistent estimator of the variance or the multiplier bootstrap applied to lwl^wlw; the latter yields simultaneous bands across event times eee, groups g~\tilde{g}g~​ or calendar periods ttt. The large-number-of-clusters requirement may be more plausible for aggregated parameters than for individual group-time effects.

Pre-Testing, Repeated Cross-Sections and Simulations

Under Assumption 3, ATT(g,t)=0ATT(g,t)=0ATT(g,t)=0 for t<g−δt<g-\deltat<g−δ. It is common to estimate these pre-treatment parameters to assess the identifying assumptions. The estimands are adapted by replacing the long difference Yt−Yg−δ−1Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}Yt​−Yg−δ−1​ by the short difference Yt−Yt−1Y_t-Y_{t-1}Yt​−Yt−1​ for all t<g−δt<g-\deltat<g−δ, and all asymptotic and bootstrap results continue to hold for the augmented vector, so the simultaneous band also covers the pre-treatment estimates. The paper treats these as a check on credibility and not as a device for selecting an assumption. Repeated cross-sections are covered in an appendix: when each period is a random sample from a population whose composition is stable over time, analogous OR, IPW and DR estimands identify ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t), with the long difference of outcomes replaced by differences of period-specific means or regressions for group ggg and the comparison group. The Monte Carlo study of finite sample performance is reported in the supplementary appendix and not in the main text.

Application: Minimum Wage and Teen Employment

The application studies 2001-2007, when the federal minimum wage was constant at 5.15 dollars per hour. The sample consists of counties in states whose minimum wage equalled the federal one at the start of the period. A group is defined by the year in which a state first raised its minimum wage (2004, 2006 or 2007; Illinois is the only state in the 2004 group), and counties in states that never raised it are the never-treated comparison group. County teen employment comes from the Quarterly Workforce Indicators and pre-treatment covariates from the 2000 County Data Book. After dropping ten states with a higher minimum wage in 2000, seven without teen employment data and four in the Northern census region, the sample has 2284 counties in 29 states. Treated and untreated counties differ: 27 percent of treated counties are in the South against 59 percent of untreated ones, mean population is 94,320 against 53,430, the white share is 0.89 against 0.83, the poverty rate 0.13 against 0.16 and median income 33,910 against 31,890 dollars. The main text uses δ=0\delta=0δ=0, the never-treated comparison group and a bootstrap clustered at the county level; results with not-yet-treated counties and one year of anticipation are reported as similar. Standard errors are in parentheses.

  • Unconditional parallel trends: the seven post-treatment group-time effects range from 2.3 to 13.6 percent lower teen employment, and five are significant. For the 2004 group the effect is −0.034-0.034−0.034 in 2004, −0.071-0.071−0.071 in 2005, −0.125-0.125−0.125 in 2006 and −0.136-0.136−0.136 in 2007; for the 2006 group it is −0.023-0.023−0.023 in 2006 and −0.071-0.071−0.071 in 2007. The simple weighted average θWO\theta^O_WθWO​ is −0.052-0.052−0.052 (0.006) and the overall parameter θselO\theta^O_{sel}θselO​ is −0.039-0.039−0.039 (0.007), close to the TWFE coefficient of −0.037-0.037−0.037 (0.006). Group-specific effects are −0.091-0.091−0.091 (0.019), −0.047-0.047−0.047 (0.008) and −0.028-0.028−0.028 (0.007) for the 2004, 2006 and 2007 groups. The event-study effects are −0.027-0.027−0.027 (0.006), −0.071-0.071−0.071 (0.009), −0.125-0.125−0.125 (0.021) and −0.136-0.136−0.136 (0.023) for exposure of zero to three years, averaging −0.090-0.090−0.090 (0.013). Calendar-time effects are −0.034-0.034−0.034, −0.071-0.071−0.071, −0.055-0.055−0.055 and −0.050-0.050−0.050 for 2004 to 2007, averaging −0.052-0.052−0.052 (0.013). The balanced event study over the 2004 and 2006 groups gives −0.027-0.027−0.027 and −0.071-0.071−0.071, averaging −0.049-0.049−0.049 (0.008).

  • Conditional parallel trends: covariates are region, population, median income, the white share, the share with a high school education and the poverty rate; the propensity score is a logit with quadratic terms in population and median income, and the outcome regression uses the same specification. A TWFE regression with unit and region-by-year fixed effects gives −0.008-0.008−0.008 (0.006), small and insignificant, as in Dube, Lester and Reich (2010). The DR estimates still indicate employment losses: group-time effects range from 0.9 percent (2006 group in 2006, insignificant) to 7.1 percent (2004 group in 2007), and three of seven are significant. θWO\theta^O_WθWO​ is −0.033-0.033−0.033 (0.007) and θselO\theta^O_{sel}θselO​ is −0.031-0.031−0.031 (0.007). Group-specific effects are −0.044-0.044−0.044 (0.020), −0.029-0.029−0.029 (0.008) and −0.029-0.029−0.029 (0.008). Event-study effects are −0.024-0.024−0.024 (0.006), −0.041-0.041−0.041 (0.009), −0.050-0.050−0.050 (0.022) and −0.071-0.071−0.071 (0.026), averaging −0.046-0.046−0.046 (0.013), so the effect still grows with exposure. Calendar-time effects are −0.030-0.030−0.030, −0.025-0.025−0.025, −0.030-0.030−0.030 and −0.049-0.049−0.049, averaging −0.033-0.033−0.033 (0.012), and the balanced event study gives −0.016-0.016−0.016 and −0.041-0.041−0.041, averaging −0.028-0.028−0.028 (0.008).

  • Computation and caveats: all group-time effects with 1000 bootstrap iterations take 3.0 seconds on a laptop. Some pre-treatment pseudo effects differ significantly from zero, which is suggestive evidence against parallel trends, and the size of the minimum wage increase differs across states. The authors' main conclusion is that, holding the identifying assumptions fixed, the choice of estimation method can change conclusions qualitatively in an application with heterogeneous and dynamic effects and staggered adoption.

  • Callaway, Brantly and Pedro HC Sant’Anna. 2021. “Difference-in-differences with multiple time periods.” Journal of Econometrics, 225(2): 200–230.

The generalized propensity score is an ordinary binary propensity score computed inside a subpopulation. The conditioning event Gg+(1−Ds)(1−Gg)=1G_g+(1-D_s)(1-G_g)=1Gg​+(1−Ds​)(1−Gg​)=1 selects the units that either belong to group ggg (so Gg=1G_g=1Gg​=1) or are outside group ggg and still untreated in period sss (so Ds=0D_s=0Ds​=0 and Gg=0G_g=0Gg​=0). The two cases exclude each other, so the sum of the two indicators is again an indicator. By the definition of a conditional probability,

pg,s(X)=P(Gg=1∣X)P(Gg=1∣X)+P(Ds=0,Gg=0∣X)p_{g,s}(X)=\frac{P(G_g=1|X)}{P(G_g=1|X)+P(D_s=0,G_g=0|X)}pg,s​(X)=P(Gg​=1∣X)+P(Ds​=0,Gg​=0∣X)P(Gg​=1∣X)​

so pg,s(X)p_{g,s}(X)pg,s​(X) is the share of group ggg among group ggg plus the comparison units available at sss, for units with covariates XXX.

The second equality in the equation is an identity and not a new definition. Under irreversibility 1−DT=C1-D_{\mathcal{T}}=C1−DT​=C, and a never-treated unit cannot belong to a group g≤Tg\leq\mathcal{T}g≤T, hence

(1−DT)(1−Gg)=C(1−Gg)=C(1-D_{\mathcal{T}})(1-G_g)=C(1-G_g)=C(1−DT​)(1−Gg​)=C(1−Gg​)=C

and the conditioning event at s=Ts=\mathcal{T}s=T is Gg+C=1G_g+C=1Gg​+C=1.

What is used later is the odds:

pg(X)1−pg(X)=P(Gg=1∣X)P(C=1∣X),pg,s(X)1−pg,s(X)=P(Gg=1∣X)P(Ds=0,Gg=0∣X)\frac{p_g(X)}{1-p_g(X)}=\frac{P(G_g=1|X)}{P(C=1|X)},\qquad\frac{p_{g,s}(X)}{1-p_{g,s}(X)}=\frac{P(G_g=1|X)}{P(D_s=0,G_g=0|X)}1−pg​(X)pg​(X)​=P(C=1∣X)P(Gg​=1∣X)​,1−pg,s​(X)pg,s​(X)​=P(Ds​=0,Gg​=0∣X)P(Gg​=1∣X)​

These odds are the weights that give the comparison units the covariate distribution of group ggg in equations (7), (9) and (10). Overlap (Assumption 6) keeps the score below one, so the odds are finite; no lower bound is needed because the target is an effect on the treated. A numerical illustration without covariates: if group ggg is a share 0.20.20.2 of the population and the never-treated units a share 0.50.50.5, then pg=0.2/0.7≈0.29p_g=0.2/0.7\approx0.29pg​=0.2/0.7≈0.29 and the odds are 0.40.40.4.

This is the observation rule that links the data to the potential outcomes. For each unit exactly one of the indicators Gi,2,…,Gi,TG_{i,2},\dots,G_{i,\mathcal{T}}Gi,2​,…,Gi,T​ equals one, or none does (a never-treated unit). The rule therefore reads

Yi,t={Yi,t(0)if Gi=∞Yi,t(g)if Gi=gY_{i,t}=\begin{cases}Y_{i,t}(0)&\text{if }G_i=\infty\\Y_{i,t}(g)&\text{if }G_i=g\end{cases}Yi,t​={Yi,t​(0)Yi,t​(g)​if Gi​=∞if Gi​=g​

for every period ttt, including the periods before ggg. The sum starts at g=2g=2g=2 because nobody is treated in period 1 (Assumption 1).

Three features matter. First, the potential outcome is indexed by the adoption date only; with an absorbing treatment the adoption date determines the whole treatment path, so no further indices are needed. Second, Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​(0) is the outcome under never being treated through period T\mathcal{T}T, and it is not the same object as "not yet treated at ttt". A unit of group ggg observed at t<gt<gt<g shows Yi,t(g)Y_{i,t}(g)Yi,t​(g), which may differ from Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​(0) if the unit anticipates the treatment; equation (4) is the assumption that closes this gap in expectation. Third, for a never-treated unit the observed outcome is Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​(0) in every period, which is why that group is a clean comparison group.

The rule is used in the last step of the derivation of equation (11): for group ggg it turns Yt(g)Y_t(g)Yt​(g) into the observed YtY_tYt​, and for the comparison units it turns Yt(0)Y_t(0)Yt​(0) into the observed YtY_tYt​. The effect of the treatment on a unit of group ggg at time ttt is Yi,t(g)−Yi,t(0)Y_{i,t}(g)-Y_{i,t}(0)Yi,t​(g)−Yi,t​(0), whose second term is never observed for t≥gt\geq gt≥g.

ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t) is the mean of the unit-level effect Yt(g)−Yt(0)Y_t(g)-Y_t(0)Yt​(g)−Yt​(0) over the units first treated in period ggg, evaluated in calendar period ttt. The first index fixes who is averaged (a cohort), the second fixes when the effect is measured. With T\mathcal{T}T periods there can be up to (T−1)×T(\mathcal{T}-1)\times\mathcal{T}(T−1)×T such parameters; those with t≥gt\geq gt≥g are post-treatment effects with exposure e=t−ge=t-ge=t−g, and those with t<gt<gt<g are anticipation effects, which equation (4) sets to zero for t<g−δt<g-\deltat<g−δ.

By the observation rule in equation (2), the first half is a mean of data:

E[Yt(g)∣Gg=1]=E[Yt∣Gg=1]\mathbb{E}\left[Y_t(g)|G_g=1\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_t|G_g=1\right]E[Yt​(g)∣Gg​=1]=E[Yt​∣Gg​=1]

The second half, E[Yt(0)∣Gg=1]\mathbb{E}[Y_t(0)|G_g=1]E[Yt​(0)∣Gg​=1], is a counterfactual mean, and the whole identification problem consists of recovering it from the comparison group. The parameter is linked to its conditional version by iterated expectations:

ATT(g,t)=E[ATTX(g,t)∣Gg=1],ATTX(g,t)=E[Yt(g)−Yt(0)∣X,Gg=1]ATT(g,t)=\mathbb{E}\left[ATT_X(g,t)|G_g=1\right],\qquad ATT_X(g,t)=\mathbb{E}\left[Y_t(g)-Y_t(0)|X,G_g=1\right]ATT(g,t)=E[ATTX​(g,t)∣Gg​=1],ATTX​(g,t)=E[Yt​(g)−Yt​(0)∣X,Gg​=1]

which is the route taken in equations (11) and (8).

No restriction is placed on how ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t)ATT(g,t) varies with ggg or ttt; homogeneity would be a restriction such as ATT(g,t)=τATT(g,t)=\tauATT(g,t)=τ for all t≥gt\geq gt≥g. With T=2\mathcal{T}=2T=2 the only parameter is ATT(2,2)ATT(2,2)ATT(2,2), the textbook ATTATTATT. These parameters are the building blocks of every aggregate in equations (14) to (21).

Assumption 3 says that, more than δ\deltaδ periods before adoption, the mean outcome of group ggg is what it would have been had the group never been treated. It restricts conditional means only; it does not require Yt(g)=Yt(0)Y_t(g)=Y_t(0)Yt​(g)=Yt​(0) unit by unit. The horizon δ\deltaδ is in periods, is non-negative and must be known to the researcher.

Its first consequence follows by averaging over XXX within group ggg: for t<g−δt<g-\deltat<g−δ,

Nothing identifies β\betaβ as a causal parameter beyond the linear model itself. Least squares compares outcome changes of units that switch into treatment with outcome changes of all other units, and that includes units that are already treated. If effects change with exposure, the outcome change of an already-treated unit contains the change in its own effect:

These three overall parameters are simple averages of partial aggregates. The first averages the event-study parameters of equation (15) over the T−1\mathcal{T}-1T−1 possible exposures e=0,…,T−2e=0,\dots,\mathcal{T}-2e=0,…,T−2; the second averages the calendar-time parameters of equation (18) over the T−1\mathcal{T}-1T−1 periods t=2,…,Tt=2,\dots,\mathcal{T}t=2,…,T; the third averages the balanced event-study parameters of equation (16) over the e′+1e'+1e′+1 exposures 0,…,e′0,\dots,e'0,…,e′. each non-negative and summing to one, because every partial aggregate has weights summing to one.

The first gives every length of exposure the same importance, although long exposures are observed only for the earliest cohorts (θes(T−2)\theta_{es}(\mathcal{T}-2)θes​(T−2) is ATT(2,T)ATT(2,\mathcal{T})ATT(2,T) alone), so a few cohorts can dominate; the second gives every calendar period the same importance, although early periods contain few treated cohorts. Both mix cohorts differently across the terms being averaged, which is the composition problem. The third fixes the cohorts, so it is the average effect over the first e′+1e'+1e′+1 periods of exposure for cohorts observed that long, and is local to them.

This is the sample analogue of the DR estimand in equation (9), built by the analogy principle in two steps. First, the two nuisance functions are replaced by fitted parametric working models: p^g(X;π^g)\widehat{p}_g(X;\widehat{\pi}_g)p​g​(X;πg​), for example a logit of GgG_gGg​ on XXX estimated on the units with Gg+C=1G_g+C=1Gg​+C=1, and m^g,t,δnev(X;β^g,t,δnev)\widehat{m}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}(X;\widehat{\beta}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta})mg,t,δnev​(X;β​g,t,δnev​), for example a least squares regression of Yt−Yg−δ−1Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}Yt​−Yg−δ−1​ on XXX among the never-treated units. Second, population expectations are replaced by sample means En\mathbb{E}_nEn​, both the outer one and those inside the weights of equation (23).

Since the weights are normalized, the estimator is a difference of two weighted averages of regression-adjusted long differences:

ATT^drnev(g,t;δ)=En[w^gtreat(Yt−Yg−δ−1−m^g,t,δnev)]−En[w^gcomp,nev(Yt−Yg−δ−1−m^g,t,δnev)]\widehat{ATT}^{nev}_{dr}(g,t;\delta)=\mathbb{E}_n\left[\widehat{w}^{treat}_g\left(Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}-\widehat{m}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)\right]-\mathbb{E}_n\left[\widehat{w}^{comp,nev}_g\left(Y_t-Y_{g-\delta-1}-\widehat{m}^{nev}_{g,t,\delta}\right)\right]ATTdrnev​(g,t;δ)=En​[wgtreat​(Yt​−Yg−δ−1​−mg,t,δnev​)]−En​[wgcomp,nev​(Yt​−Yg−δ−1​−mg,t,δnev​)]

The first term is the mean over group ggg of the difference between each unit's change and the change predicted for it from the never-treated; this alone is the OR estimator. The second term is a weighted mean of the regression residuals of the never-treated units, with weights that mimic the covariate distribution of group ggg. If the outcome model is right, this term is close to zero; if it is wrong but the propensity score model is right, the term corrects the bias of the first. This is the finite-sample counterpart of the double robustness shown in the derivation of equation (9).

Each (g,t)(g,t)(g,t) has its own pair of first-step fits, and only units with Gg=1G_g=1Gg​=1 or C=1C=1C=1 and the two periods ttt and g−δ−1g-\delta-1g−δ−1 are used, so the estimator is a two-group, two-period DR DiD estimator applied to a subsample. Its large-sample behaviour is given in equations (24) to (26).

These are the estimated versions of the two weights in equation (9). A fitted score close to one produces a very large weight, which is the practical meaning of limited overlap.

Both weights are divided by their own sample mean (Hajek-type normalization), so in every sample

This is the delta method for the map from the weights and the group-time effects to θ\thetaθ, which is linear in each argument. Because the terms are added unit by unit before squaring, the variance E[lw(W)2]\mathbb{E}[l^w(W)^2]E[lw(W)2] automatically contains all covariances between the different (g,t)(g,t)(g,t) estimators, the factor Σ\SigmaΣ of equation (26), and between these and the estimated weights. Ignoring the weight term would understate or overstate the variance unless the weights are known. For inference one estimates lwl^wlw by plugging in w^\widehat{w}w, A^\widehat{A}A and the estimated influence functions, and either averages its square or perturbs it with multipliers as in equation (27); stacking the lwl^wlw of several aggregates (for instance θes(e)\theta_{es}(e)θes​(e) for all eee) gives simultaneous bands by the procedure of equation (28).
